content: Postpartum women are encouraged to engage in a combination of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities to support their physical health. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior for pregnant and postpartum women emphasize the importance of limiting sedentary time, as excessive sedentary behavior is associated with poor health outcomes, including increased risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity, even at light intensity, can provide significant health benefits. For pregnant and postpartum women, sedentary behavior is defined as time spent sitting or lying down with minimal energy expenditure while awake, across various settings such as work, education, home, community, or transportation. Evidence from the general adult population has been extrapolated to inform these recommendations, as direct population-specific data is limited. The findings suggest that minimizing sedentary behavior and incorporating physical activity outweigh potential risks for this group. For adults and older adults living with chronic conditions such as cancer, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or HIV, regular physical activity is strongly recommended. This includes at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination of both per week. Additionally, muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week to provide further health benefits. For older adults, incorporating balance and strength training three or more days per week is advised to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Physical activity has been shown to improve health outcomes in individuals with chronic conditions. For cancer survivors, it reduces all-cause and cancer-specific mortality and may lower the risk of recurrence. In people with hypertension, physical activity improves cardiovascular disease outcomes, physical function, and quality of life. In individuals living with HIV, physical activity enhances physical fitness, mental health, and quality of life without adversely affecting disease progression markers like CD4 count or viral load. The WHO guidelines also highlight the importance of gradually increasing physical activity levels for those unable to meet the recommended targets initially. Consulting healthcare professionals or physical activity specialists can help tailor activity plans to individual needs, abilities, and medical conditions. Evidence supports the inclusion of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities for people with chronic conditions, as these interventions provide substantial health benefits and improve overall quality of life.
